e.t: “Aaron” is a personal name, referring to the biblical man named Aaron rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears five times, including references in Luke, Acts, and Hebrews. It is rendered as “Aaron,” and once in possessive form as “Aaron’s,” when expressing connection or ownership. The surrounding passage determines what aspect of Aaron’s life or role is being discussed in each occurrence.

Verb, Present, Active, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to compete” or “to compete in a contest.” It describes active participation in a contest, emphasizing the effort of striving against others according to the contest’s requirements. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both instances appearing in 2 Timothy 2:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the central idea remains competing in an organized contest rather than merely making an attempt or expressing a desire.

This word means “recovery of sight,” describing the restoration of a person’s ability to see. It refers to sight being received again or returned, rather than merely to ordinary vision. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 4:18. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is clear: sight restored to someone who had been unable to see.

Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to overturn,” describing the action of turning something over or undoing its established position. It can refer to a physical act or to the disruption of something that has been set in place, but the precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in John, 2 Timothy, and Titus. Its central idea remains the removal or reversal of an existing position or arrangement.

me: Verb, second Aorist, Middle, Indicative, first, Plural

e.t: This word means “to renounce,” describing a deliberate refusal or rejection of something. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 4:2. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise force there cannot be described further; however, its central meaning remains the act of turning away from or disowning something. The word therefore points to a conscious break with what one refuses to accept or practice.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to make an opening in a roof” or “to unroof.” It describes the action of removing or opening part of a roof, functioning as an action word rather than naming the roof itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Mark 2:4. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of opening or uncovering a roof.

The word means “childless”: having no children. It describes a person who has no child. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both in Luke 20:28–29, and is rendered “childless” each time. The word therefore names the condition of having no children. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear.

“Berean” refers to a person from Berea, a city mentioned in the New Testament. It identifies someone by connection with that place rather than describing a character quality, belief, or occupation. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 20:4. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply a person associated with Berea.

This word means “farmer,” referring to a person who cultivates land and works with crops. It describes the agricultural worker in ordinary terms, rather than a spiritual title or special office. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times, including repeated use in Matthew 21 for the men entrusted with a vineyard. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a farmer or cultivator.

This word refers to an “old wives’ tale”—a traditional story or saying treated as unreliable or unworthy of serious attention. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:7. The word itself describes the kind of tale being dismissed, rather than naming a person or presenting a teaching to believe. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: a fanciful or foolish traditional story.

This word refers to a person from Damascus, identifying someone by connection with that city. It can be understood as “Damascene” or “from Damascus.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:32, and its meaning is geographical rather than a description of a person’s character or beliefs. The word therefore identifies a Damascene—someone associated with Damascus—without, by itself, explaining anything more about that person.

Didymus is a personal name or designation, rendered as “Didymus.” It identifies the same person wherever this Greek New Testament word appears. The word occurs three times, all in John: John 11:16, John 20:24, and John 21:2. Since the available wording gives the name but no further definition, its central function is to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what that person is doing in each passage.

This word means “glory,” referring to honor, splendor, or a state of exalted greatness. In the Greek New Testament, it is used especially for the glory belonging to God, revealed through Christ, and promised to those who share in what God gives. It can also describe the visible magnificence associated with earthly kingdoms or the future appearing of Christ. The word occurs 166 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that glory is a recurring biblical theme rather than a rare or specialized idea.

me: Verb, Imperfect, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to carry out,” describing the action of taking something through or bringing it out. It is an action word rather than a name for a person, place, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 7:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic idea remains the carrying out or bringing forth of something.

me: Verb, peRfect, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to fulfill”—to bring something to completion or carry it out as required. It is an action word describing the completion of an expressed purpose, promise, or expectation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the carrying out or completion of what was intended.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “in Greek.” It identifies Greek as the language being used, written, or understood in a statement. It functions as a language expression rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in John 19:20 and Acts 21:37. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being spoken or written in Greek, but the word itself points plainly to the Greek language.

This word means “authority”: the right, power, or recognized freedom to act, command, or decide. It can describe authority exercised by a person, granted to someone, or held over others. In the Greek New Testament, it is used broadly, appearing 102 times, so its exact expression depends on the sentence—sometimes focusing on the right to act and sometimes on the power being exercised. Its central idea remains authority: a legitimate ability or right to direct events, make decisions, or carry out an action.

e.t: This word means “to rebuke”: to speak firmly against someone’s words or actions, correcting or restraining them. It describes a direct verbal response rather than a quiet feeling or private judgment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 29 times, including scenes where Jesus addresses danger, wrong understanding, or disruptive behavior. Its basic sense remains a firm call to stop, correct, or heed a warning; the surrounding passage shows whether the rebuke is directed toward a person, a spiritual power, or a threatening situation.

This word describes something that is pleasing or well-pleasing—something regarded favorably and accepted with approval. In the Greek New Testament, it is used nine times, including language about conduct, service, and what a person seeks to offer. Its basic sense is positive: it identifies that which gives satisfaction or meets an approving standard. The surrounding sentence determines who regards it as pleasing and what action or offering is being described.

This word means “foundation”: the supporting base on which a building rests, and, by extension, the underlying basis on which something is established. In the New Testament, it is used for physical foundations as well as foundational work or structure. It occurs 16 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Luke, Acts, Paul’s letters, Hebrews, and Revelation. Its central idea remains a firm underlying support, whether the reference is to a structure or to what gives something lasting stability.

This word means clothing—what a person wears. It refers to garments as physical items, whether worn, carried, or placed on someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 60 times, showing regular use for ordinary clothing rather than an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its basic meaning remains clothing or garments.

e.t: The word means “to cover”: to place something over another thing so it is covered. It describes the action of covering rather than the object used for covering. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all within two verses in 1 Corinthians 11. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the act of covering. The word should therefore be understood according to this basic action, without adding a broader meaning not present in the context.

e.t: This word means to be treacherous or to deal treacherously with someone. It describes deceitful, unfaithful, or harmful treatment rather than honest dealing. As an action word, it focuses on what a person does toward another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is acting deceptively or betraying another person’s trust.

This word means “coin” or “coins,” referring to money in a physical, countable form. It functions as a noun and names the objects themselves rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 2:15. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic meaning is money represented by individual coins.

e.t: This word means to steal—to take something that belongs to another, usually secretly or wrongfully. It is an action word describing the act itself, and it may be rendered as “steal,” “steals,” “to steal,” or as a question, “do you steal.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times in 11 verses, showing a repeated term for dishonest taking rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The word means “better,” describing something as superior in quality, condition, or outcome compared with something else. It expresses improvement or advantage rather than merely identifying an object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 4:52; the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is being compared in that particular setting. Its basic sense is a comparative judgment of greater goodness or benefit.

This word means “storm”—a violent disturbance of the weather. It is a noun used for a storm as an actual natural event, not merely a general difficulty or troubling situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including accounts involving the sea and a comparison involving empty, unstable people. The central idea remains a powerful, turbulent storm. The surrounding passage determines the precise force of each occurrence, but the word itself directly names the storm. Its English rendering is consistently “storm.”

This word means “winepress,” the place or device where grapes are crushed so their juice flows out. It names a physical feature associated with making wine, rather than the wine itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, appearing once in Matthew and four times in Revelation. Its repeated use in Revelation reflects imagery involving a winepress, but the word’s basic meaning remains the grape-pressing place or trough. Magog is a proper name, referring to a named figure, people, or place rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Revelation 20:8, and is rendered “Magog.” The word itself does not describe a general concept such as faith, judgment, or strength; its meaning is its identification of Magog. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the specific role the name has in that verse.

e.t: This word means “to be drunk” or “to get drunk,” describing becoming affected by intoxicating drink. It focuses on the condition or action of becoming drunk rather than merely mentioning alcohol. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages that address drunkenness as a recognizable human behavior. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains becoming or being intoxicated.

This word means “hired worker” or “hired workers”—a person or group employed to work in return for wages. It refers to workers engaged for service rather than identifying a family member or owner. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 15. The plural wording can describe more than one such worker, while the central idea remains paid employment. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to people hired to perform work.

e.t: This word means “few” or “little,” describing a small number or a small amount. It can refer to people, things, or quantity, depending on what it describes in the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 40 times across 39 verses, with both “few” and “little” representing its central sense. Its precise reference—whether to number or amount—comes from the surrounding words and passage. The word appears throughout the New Testament, including Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts, and 1 Peter.

This word means the ear or ears—the bodily organs used for hearing. It normally refers to the physical ear, whether speaking of one ear or both. In the New Testament, it occurs 36 times across 34 verses, often in statements about hearing, listening, or having ears attentive to what is said. The word can therefore point to the physical organ while also serving in appeals to hear and understand. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “with all the house” or “with one’s whole family.” It describes something done or experienced together with everyone belonging to a household, rather than by one person alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 16:34. Its basic sense is therefore household-wide inclusion: the statement concerns the entire family or household group accompanying or sharing in the action. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s specific force there.

The word refers to “Patara,” a proper name in the Greek New Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or person; it identifies a named place. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 21:1. Its basic meaning is simply the place-name Patara, while the word’s particular significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and context.

This word describes a “wanderer” or something “wandering”—moving without a settled course or destination. It can identify a person who roams or describe movement that lacks direction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:13, so its broader use must be understood from this basic sense rather than from several biblical examples. The word emphasizes unsettled movement and the absence of a fixed path.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to call” or “to summon,” describing an intentional invitation or command for someone to come. It may refer to calling people together, bringing someone near, or addressing someone so they respond. The central idea is directed calling rather than a casual mention. It occurs 29 times in the Greek New Testament, showing regular use for people being called or summoned in different situations.

me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to flow” or “to overflow,” describing something moving onward like a stream or water pouring out. It expresses continuous movement rather than a fixed condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 7:38, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The basic idea remains movement that proceeds outward, with “overflow” highlighting abundance or fullness when the context calls for it.

This word means “to be unsettled” or “to shake.” It describes being disturbed, agitated, or moved from steadiness rather than remaining calm and secure. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 3:3. Its basic sense concerns a person being shaken or unsettled, while the surrounding verse determines the particular nature of that disturbance. The meaning is therefore broader than physical movement alone and can describe inward instability or distress.

This word means “moth-eaten,” describing something damaged or consumed by moths. It refers to the wasting away of stored clothing or other valuable fabric, making the item spoiled and no longer sound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in James 5:2. The word itself names the physical condition rather than explaining the surrounding warning or teaching; its fuller force in that passage comes from the verse and its context.

This word means “cross” or “crosses,” referring to the cross as an object. In the New Testament, it is used both for the physical cross associated with Jesus’ death and in expressions about carrying or bearing a cross. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it is used across several books and contexts while retaining this central meaning.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This verb means “to live in luxury” or “to revel,” describing a life of lavish pleasure and self-indulgence. It expresses more than simply having possessions: it points to enjoying comfort and excess in a celebratory, pleasure-seeking way. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Revelation 18. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is luxurious, self-indulgent living.

This word describes someone who inherits together with another person—a co-heir or joint heir. It expresses shared participation in an inheritance rather than receiving it alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Romans, Ephesians, Hebrews, and 1 Peter. Its central idea remains the same across these uses: people are joined as fellow recipients of what is inherited. The exact inheritance and relationship involved are determined by the surrounding passage.

Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, second, Plural

e.t: This word describes the act of accusing someone falsely or extorting from them. It points to dishonest treatment in which a person uses accusations or pressure to obtain something wrongfully. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke, so its meaning is concentrated in a small number of passages rather than spread broadly across the New Testament. The central idea remains wrongful accusation or taking advantage of others for gain.

This word means “four thousand,” referring to a quantity of 4,000. It is a number word used to count people or objects, rather than to describe a quality, action, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times: four times in Matthew and Mark and once in Acts. Its uses include numbered groups and a numbered military force, but the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being counted in each case.

This word means “deceiver”—someone who misleads others rather than dealing with them truthfully. It identifies a person by the harmful effect of his words or influence: he leads people away from what is true. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Titus 1:10. The reference identifies where the word appears, but its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage and verse text.

This word means “voice,” “sound,” or “noise”—something heard, whether produced by a person or arising as an audible sound. It can refer to one voice or to voices together, and its exact sense is shaped by what is making the sound and how it functions in the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 139 times, so it is used broadly for audible speech and other sounds rather than for only one special kind of utterance.

“Hosanna!” is an exclamation preserved in English as “Hosanna!” It functions as a spoken cry rather than as a description of a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times in five verses, occurring in Matthew, Mark, and John. Because the word is presented as an exclamation and no fuller definition is given here, its central meaning is best stated simply: “Hosanna!” The surrounding verse supplies the particular force of the cry in each passage.
